title: Template Method Pattern
summary: Sharing an algorithm's skeleton in a base class while letting subclasses fill in the steps that genuinely differ, without duplicating the parts that don't.

slides.markdown:
**Template Method** puts the fixed skeleton of an algorithm — its overall sequence of steps — in a base class, and lets subclasses override only the steps that actually vary. Importing a CSV and importing a JSON file both follow "read file → parse → validate → save," but *parsing* and *validating* differ per format.

Instead of copy-pasting that four-step sequence into a `CsvImporter` and a `JsonImporter` and duplicating the read/save steps, the base class owns the sequence once and calls out to subclass-specific `parse()`/`validate()` methods.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem: several algorithms share the same skeleton but differ in steps
slides.markdown:
A `CsvImporter` and a `JsonImporter` both do: read the file, parse it into records, validate each record, save valid records to the database. Written independently, both classes duplicate the read-file and save-to-database logic verbatim — only `parse()` and `validate()` actually differ by format.

That duplication is a maintenance trap: if the save step needs a bug fix (say, wrapping it in a transaction), you now edit it in both classes, and a third `XmlImporter` means a third copy-paste. Worse, nothing enforces that every importer follows the same sequence — a future importer could accidentally validate before parsing, or skip validation entirely.

The underlying problem: the *sequence* of steps is genuinely shared, but naive duplication re-implements the sequence every time, obscuring that shared structure.

slides.sectionTitle: Template Method: define the skeleton in a base class, defer steps to subclasses
slides.markdown:
An abstract `DataImporter` base class defines one concrete method, `import()`, that calls `readFile()`, `this.parse(contents)`, `this.validate(records)`, `saveToDb(records)` in that fixed order. `readFile()` and `saveToDb()` are implemented once, in the base class, shared by everyone. `parse()` and `validate()` are declared abstract — each subclass *must* implement them, but can't change the order they're called in.

`CsvImporter` only ever writes `parse()` and `validate()` for CSV; it inherits `import()` and the shared steps for free, and cannot accidentally call things out of order because it doesn't control the sequence at all.

The base class owns *control* of the algorithm; subclasses only own the *steps* they're explicitly given a hook for.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a base-class algorithm with hook methods overridden by subclasses
slides.markdown:
The base class's one concrete method calls a fixed sequence of steps; some are implemented in the base class itself (shared), others are abstract "hooks" that only exist as declarations until a subclass fills them in.

Calling `csvImporter.import()` runs code that's 90% defined in the base class and 10% supplied by the subclass, but the *caller* only ever calls the one template method.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a DataImporter template with parse()/validate() steps overridden per format
The Hollywood Principle: "don't call us, we'll call you"
slides.markdown:
Template Method is the textbook example of the **Hollywood Principle**: subclasses don't call the base class's logic — the base class calls *them*, at exactly the points it decides. `CsvImporter` never invokes `import()`'s internal sequence itself; it just implements the hooks and waits to be called by the framework it inherits from.

This inverts the usual direction of control in inheritance, where a subclass typically calls `super.method()` and adds its own logic around it. Here, the subclass has no say over *when* or *in what order* its own methods run — that decision belongs entirely to the base class's template method.

The practical upshot: a subclass can't accidentally break the sequence, because it was never given control of the sequence to begin with.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: Template Method vs Strategy — inheritance-based vs composition-based step variation
slides.markdown:
| | Template Method | Strategy |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Inheritance — subclass overrides specific steps of a fixed algorithm | Composition — a whole algorithm object is swapped at runtime |
| What varies | Individual steps inside one fixed sequence | The entire algorithm, as one unit |
| Runtime flexibility | Fixed at compile time — a `CsvImporter` is always a `CsvImporter` | An object can hold a different Strategy at any time |
| Multiple inheritance-like variation | Awkward — can't easily mix steps from two subclasses | Easy — swap in any combination of strategy objects |

**How to decide:** if the algorithm's *shape* is genuinely fixed and only specific steps vary, Template Method's simplicity and guaranteed sequencing win. If you need to swap the *entire* algorithm at runtime, or the same object needs different behavior at different times, use Strategy instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a template so rigid a new subclass ends up overriding almost everything
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Once I've defined the template method's sequence, every future subclass will naturally fit it."

**Why it's wrong:** if a new format — say, importing from a streaming API instead of a file — genuinely doesn't fit "read file → parse → validate → save" (there's no single file to read, records arrive incrementally), forcing it into `DataImporter` means overriding `readFile()` to do something unrelated to reading a file, or overriding `import()` itself, which defeats the whole point of a fixed template. A subclass that overrides most of the base class's steps is a sign the shared skeleton was never actually shared by this case.

**Correct model:** if a new case needs to override the bulk of the template's steps just to shoehorn itself in, that's a signal to stop forcing it into the hierarchy — either the base class's skeleton needs to be redesigned to genuinely fit both cases, or the new case belongs in its own class using a different pattern (Strategy composed differently) rather than inheriting from a template it barely fits.
